analysis.one_liner: Required derivatives market makers to register with the Treasury and imposed transparency, margin, and anti-fraud rules on derivatives trading.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in either committee or on the House floor and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up the first registration system for firms that make markets in derivatives — the complex financial contracts whose unregulated trading contributed to the 2008 financial crisis. It would have directed the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to write rules requiring disclosure of who is trading what, minimum margin (up-front collateral) requirements, and anti-fraud standards, and given those agencies power to fine violators and force them to give back improper gains. Companies using derivatives simply to hedge their own business risks would have been exempt from registration, and the Treasury Secretary would have had power to block regulators' rules that did not fit a uniform framework. The bill was sent to two House committees and never came out.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would have benefited from a derivatives market that was harder to use for fraud and manipulation, easier for regulators to monitor through an audit trail of trades, and less likely to produce a repeat of the unregulated credit default swap losses that nearly brought down AIG in 2008 — losses that helped trigger the recession, job losses, and bailouts that followed [S3]. Honest market participants would have gained from clearer rules and a level playing field, since violators faced fines of up to $1.5 million per violation, cease-and-desist orders, and forced repayment of improper gains [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people exposed to financial crises

how_it_helps.text: It created an Office of Derivatives Supervision in the Treasury to coordinate the SEC and CFTC and to oversee registration of derivatives market makers [S2][S3].

It required the SEC and CFTC to write rules mandating disclosure of derivatives positions, an audit trail identifying who traded what and when, anti-fraud and truth-in-marketing standards, and minimum margin and collateral requirements [S2][S3].
It gave the SEC and CFTC power to impose civil penalties of up to $1.5 million per violation for fraud or manipulation, issue cease-and-desist orders, and force violators to disgorge gains [S3].

It required standardized derivatives traded between the largest market participants to go through clearinghouses, which stand between both sides of a trade and reduce the risk that one default cascades through the system [S3].
It made fraud, deception, and manipulation in derivatives trading unlawful and required registered traders to have policies preventing misuse of inside information [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firms that make markets in derivatives — largely large banks and financial institutions — would have borne registration requirements, margin and collateral rules, disclosure and audit-trail obligations, and the risk of civil penalties up to $1.5 million per violation [S2][S3]. Treasury and the two regulators would have needed new funding, which Congress was authorized to appropriate [S3]. Companies that hedge with derivatives were largely spared: they were excluded from registration and could trade with limited or no margin [S3].

drawbacks.text: The Treasury Secretary could block any SEC or CFTC derivatives rule that the Office determined did not 'harmonize' commodities and securities regulation, concentrating a veto over financial regulators in a department that also oversees the banking system [S3].

The bill excluded companies that use derivatives to hedge their own business risks from the registration requirement, and permitted trades between a major dealer and a creditworthy customer to carry limited or no margin, so a large slice of the market would have faced little direct oversight [S3].

Civil penalties were capped at $300,000 for individuals and $1.5 million for firms even in the most serious fraud cases — amounts that are small relative to the size of the trades and the losses at issue, which may have limited the deterrent effect [S3].
The stricter capital and margin requirements applied only to 'major market participants' designated by the regulators, leaving smaller derivatives traders subject to lighter treatment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits were real: registration of the firms that make markets in derivatives, an audit trail of trades, margin and collateral rules, and penalty authority for the SEC and CFTC [S2][S3]. But it was a modest version of derivatives regulation. It left out companies that hedge, allowed the Treasury Secretary to veto regulators' rules, applied the toughest capital requirements only to the largest participants, and capped penalties well below the scale of the losses that the 2008 crisis demonstrated [S3]. An honest supporter would acknowledge that these carve-outs left much of the market lightly supervised. In the event, the weighing never got tested: the bill never received a vote of any kind [S1][S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees when introduced, sat there for nearly a year and a half, got sent to a subcommittee in June 2010, and died when the Congress ended without anyone ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael McMahon introduced the bill on July 22, 2009 with 13 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and the House Agriculture Committee, which share jurisdiction over derivatives [S5].

The bill would have created an Office of Derivatives Supervision in the Treasury, required derivatives market makers to register, and directed the SEC and CFTC to write rules on trade disclosure, audit trails, anti-fraud standards, and minimum margin [S3].
On June 22, 2010, the Agriculture Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management — the last recorded action [S5].
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Derivatives dealers and other traders avoided the registration, disclosure, and margin requirements the bill would have imposed on them; the public did not get the transparency and anti-fraud rules it promised, and derivatives regulation instead took shape through other legislation.

for.name: Rep. Michael E. McMahon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 22, 2009 to create a derivatives registration and oversight system [S1][S3].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further recorded action — no markup, no vote, no report to the floor [S5].

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee in June 2010 and never reported it out [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever recorded the chamber's position; all 14 supporters on record (the sponsor plus 13 cosponsors) were Democrats, and no member is on record opposing the bill.

industries.industry: Derivatives dealers and major investment banks
industries.note: The bill imposed registration, disclosure, audit-trail, margin, and penalty requirements on firms that make markets in derivatives — a real cost. But it also carved out hedgers from registration, allowed the Treasury Secretary to veto regulators' rules, applied the strictest capital requirements only to the largest participants, and let creditworthy customers trade with little or no margin, softening the burden considerably [S3].

industries.industry: Hedging end-users (nonfinancial companies using derivatives to manage business risk)
industries.note: The bill excluded anyone buying or selling derivatives to hedge an exposure or make an investment from the 'derivatives trader' registration requirement, and allowed trades between major dealers and customers who can borrow uncollateralized to carry limited or no margin [S3]. The bill's own findings argued that forcing companies to post cash collateral would drain money from their core business [S3].

industries.industry: Derivatives clearinghouses, exchanges, and trade depositories
industries.note: The bill required standardized derivatives between major participants to be cleared through clearinghouses and uncleared over-the-counter trades to be processed through a trade depository, routing more business through these institutions [S3].
